chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhl from Mufaddal ibn Salih from Layth ibn al-Bakhtari al-Muradi said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): How many menstrual periods does a slave woman count from the man's divorce? He said: 'One menstrual period.'

This does not contradict the first report, because we have clarified that the consideration is by the menstrual period (qur') when the considered factor is the menstrual period. With one menstrual period, two menstrual periods are completed: the one in which he divorced her and the one after it. And his saying (peace be upon him) in the previous report 'her waiting period is two menstrual periods' means if she entered the second menstrual period, then she has been divorced according to what we presented regarding the waiting period of a free woman.

And if a man divorces his wife and she is a slave woman and then she is freed, if it is a revocable divorce (talaq raj'i) in which the man has the right of return, it becomes obligatory upon her to observe the waiting period of a free woman. And if it is an irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in) in which he does not have the right of return, then upon her is the waiting period of slave women.

(469) 68 That is indicated by what was narrated: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a slave woman who was under a man, he divorced her and then she was freed, he said: 'She observes the waiting period of a free woman.'

key_terms.عِدَّةُ الْحُرَّةِ: Waiting period of a free woman

ai.seo_question: What is the waiting period for a slave woman upon divorce and how does it change if she is freed?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the legal nuance of a slave woman's *iddah* by equating her single menstrual period to the two periods required for a free woman, thereby harmonizing apparent textual contradictions. It further establishes the principle of status-based transition: if freed during a revocable divorce, she adopts the free woman's waiting period, whereas an irrevocable divorce retains the slave's shorter duration, reflecting the juristic interplay between manumission and marital status.
